body: Maybe plan 39 eases this pain?  If waves can be deliverables, then when a wave sets the delivery flag, then the following waves will take the latest of master.  Right?  Or is it continuing on the branch that it delivered.  Maybe this begs more thought in plan 39 and we should reopen 39.  What do you think?

anchor.quote: The design instead has the operator hand the harness a file and the harness place it

body: Sounds like this is meant to be done while the harness is in-flight.  Can it also be done when there is no other harness running?
I love this aspect and since it is a CLI command, an agent (who might be writing the script/code to be injected) can insert it during the harness' run JIT.
Make sure that this injection ability is clearly documented for agents to know about.  Either/and in a skill or the README's CLI command-line options.

Checked the code rather than guessed, and the factual answer is NO — which is exactly why you are right that it needs more thought.

Scheduler drains each wave's DAG on the 'CONTINUOUS plan branch' (:774 and :915), and a run has 'ONE integration handle / plan branch, and ONE journal' (:203). So after a wave delivers, the following waves keep going on that same plan branch. They do NOT re-base onto master and do NOT pick up anything else that landed there.

So plan 39 as written does NOT ease this pain. Delivery is one-directional: plan branch -> master.

But your instinct points at something real, and it is a genuinely open design question for 39: SHOULD a delivering wave also merge master back INTO the plan branch? If it did, the run would re-sync at each delivery barrier and #373's problem would partly dissolve — a file committed to master mid-run would reach every wave after the next barrier.

The cost is not small, and it is why I would not just add it:

- The run's base would move underneath it for reasons unrelated to the plan. A wave that went green could go red at the next barrier because of somebody else's commit, and the run would be reporting on a tree nobody chose.
- It cuts against the isolation the worktree model exists to provide, and against the stable-base assumption underneath PlanDefinitionHash and the executed-definition-divergence machinery.
- It makes 'what did this run actually verify?' harder to answer after the fact.

There is a middle option worth putting on the table: re-sync ONLY when the delivering merge is a fast-forward — i.e. master has not moved independently — which is free of surprise, and fall back to today's behaviour when it has.

So: yes, let us REOPEN 39 with this as a fourth question. It is a better place for it than 40, because it is about what the delivery boundary means, and 40 should keep working whether or not 39 ever ships.

Yes — and it is the case that matters most, so the design leads with it in section 1 ('There are TWO drain boundaries, and the second one is the important one').

  run still executing   -> drained at the next TASK BOUNDARY
  run HALTED and exited -> drained at RUN START, on the next 'guardrails run', before scheduling

The measured incident IS the second row: task 02-vendor-mermaid-runtime settled needs-human and the run EXITED, so at the moment the operator has the file in hand there is no live run to have a boundary.

Worth saying plainly because my first draft got it wrong in exactly the direction you are probing: I specified 'supply' to REFUSE when no run was in progress, which would have refused the only case anyone reaches for it in. It now refuses only when there is no RESUMABLE run at all — no journal, or a journal whose every task has settled.

The resume-path drain is also the cleaner of the two boundaries: it happens before the first task is scheduled, so nothing is branched from the base yet.

Agreed on the value, and I want to name the hazard that comes with it before it gets built, because it is not obvious and it is serious.

'supply' being a CLI command means anything that can run a shell can call it — including a TASK AGENT mid-run, which is the JIT case you are describing. That is genuinely useful for an agent authoring a script it then needs on the base. But it is also a WRITE-SCOPE BYPASS: the write-scope gate is what stops a task editing files it does not own, and a task that can call 'guardrails supply' can put any file onto the run's base without its writeScope being consulted. Every downstream check then runs over a tree containing content no task was authorised to produce.

That is the same shape as the escape hatches the harness already refuses — it is why the tool-permission layer will not let an agent write under .claude/ directly, and why 'needsHarnessWrite' exists as a supervised alternative.

Three options, and this belongs as a question rather than something I decide:

1. supply is OPERATOR-ONLY — refuse when invoked from inside a run's task environment (detectable: the task worktree sets GUARDRAILS_* env). An agent that needs a file emits needsHuman, as today.
2. supply is agent-callable but SCOPED — a task may only supply paths inside its own writeScope, which makes it a convenience rather than a hole.
3. supply is agent-callable and unrestricted — simplest, and I would argue against it.

Option 2 is the interesting one for your case: an agent writing a script it needs on the base almost certainly owns that path already, so scoping costs it nothing and closes the bypass. I will add this as a fourth question rather than pick.

Also worth noting: whichever way this goes, the provenance record in section 4 becomes more important, not less. If an agent can supply, 'what is in this tree that no task authored?' is a question the terminal gate and the #453 triage will genuinely need answered.

But each wave also has its own pre-flight checks.  Right?  Therefore, post-delivery waves should provide the types of checks (like "all tests are passing") that are typically in the pre-flight checks of a full harness run.

Yes, waves do have their own preflights, and this is a better answer than the one I wrote into 39 §1c. I have checked the mechanism and it holds — with one caveat that turns out to matter.

CONFIRMED: RunWaveEntryGateAsync (Scheduler:1391) runs a wave's ENTRY preflight against the plan-branch HEAD — 'the materialized prior wave' — per SSOT §14.3. So the seam you are pointing at is real and already built.

And it is the RIGHT seam, for a reason worth stating: it fixes the attribution problem, not just the detection one. A refresh (or a plain stale base) puts content into the tree that no task authored. If that content is broken, the wave EXIT gate goes red and the failure lands on a wave that did nothing wrong. Asserting the baseline at wave ENTRY makes the same defect fail before any task runs, where it reads correctly as 'the tree was already red on arrival'. That is #181/#182's positive-baseline archetype — never build on red — applied at the wave barrier instead of only at plan start.

THE CAVEAT, and it is a real one. The entry gate is SKIP-ONCE by design: 'a passed entry marker for this wave is not re-evaluated on resume (a negative-baseline entry check runs exactly once)'. That is correct for what it was built for — a TDD-red baseline asserting the thing does not exist yet is a fact about a moment, and re-running it after the work is done would fail.

A POSITIVE baseline is the opposite animal. 'All tests pass' is a fact about the tree AS IT IS NOW, and after a delivery or a refresh the tree has changed — so skip-once would silently pass a wave over a tree it never checked. Note the asymmetry already in the model: the wave EXIT gate is 'always re-evaluated on the current HEAD' (SSOT §14.6), and entry is not. Your proposal lands on the side that skips.

So it works, and it needs the entry gate to distinguish the two baseline kinds — a positive one re-evaluates, a negative one keeps skip-once. That is a small change and it is now the design's recommendation.

Second, smaller: a wave with no authored preflights returns Pass immediately (Scheduler:1394). The check only exists if plan-breakdown emits it, so this has to be a breakdown-side rule for delivering waves, not just a harness capability.

Folding both into 39 §1c, and it changes what I recommend there — the refresh question stops being 'is a refresh safe?' and becomes 'a refresh is safe BECAUSE the next wave re-verifies its baseline'.
